modules.title: Prompt engineering
modules.description: Write prompts that make the task, the boundaries, and the desired output clear.

lessons.title: Prompt anatomy & reusable patterns
lessons.content:
## Anatomy of a useful prompt
A useful prompt states the task, gives the context needed to do it, and names the desired output format. A concrete instruction like “Return three bullet points for a beginner” is more testable than “Make this good.” Constraints describe what not to do and how much to produce.

## Few-shot examples
Few-shot prompting includes a small number of input–output examples. Use examples to demonstrate the pattern or format, not to sneak in extra rules. Choose a normal case and one edge case so the model sees how the format holds up when input is unusual.

## Delimiters and untrusted input
Delimiters mark where reference data begins and ends. The trusted system message defines what the application does; user text and attached documents stay in an untrusted data field. Delimiters help the model see the boundary but do not replace validation and permissions.

## Iterating with a rubric
Change one part of the prompt at a time, then compare it on the same test cases. An explicit rubric can score whether a response matches the requested format and stays within the available evidence.

question.prompt: Which prompt element states what shape the answer should take?
Why supply a few input–output examples?
question.answer: To demonstrate the desired pattern or format.
question.rubric: Credit answers explaining that examples show the expected structure or behavior; a vague claim that they improve everything is insufficient.

question.prompt: Where should a document supplied by a learner go?

modules.title: LLM APIs
modules.description: Work with messages, structured responses, streaming, and safe failure recovery.

lessons.title: Structured outputs with LLM APIs
lessons.content:
## Server-side requests
An application keeps model credentials on its server. The browser sends a bounded request to the server, which checks the learner’s session and quota before calling the API. Never put private provider credentials in public JavaScript.

## JSON schema and validation
Structured output asks the provider for JSON matching a declared schema. A JSON schema can specify property names and expected types. Always validate the returned object on the server, and separately check business rules such as whether an ID exists.

## Streaming and first token
A streaming response sends small chunks as the model generates text. Time to first token measures how long the learner waits before seeing the first usable text, not how long the entire response takes. A stream should handle interruption and show incomplete output as such.

## Timeout, retry, and backoff
Retry transient failures such as rate limits or temporary server errors with bounded exponential backoff and jitter. Avoid retrying invalid credentials or malformed requests. After streaming has shown text, do not silently replay the request.

question.prompt: What still needs checking after a response matches a JSON schema?
options: Business rules such as whether IDs exist
question.answer: Business rules such as whether IDs exist

question.prompt: What does time to first token measure?
question.answer: Time until the first usable response text is visible.
question.rubric: Require the delay to the first generated text, not the full response time.

question.prompt: Which error is a good candidate for bounded retry?

modules.title: Retrieval-augmented generation
modules.description: Find useful evidence in lesson material before generating an answer.

lessons.title: Grounding answers with RAG
lessons.content:
## Retrieval before generation
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) looks up passages related to a question before a model writes an answer. The application sends only the most relevant retrieved passages, along with the question, so the answer can draw on the lesson rather than general recall. Retrieval finds evidence; generation explains it.

## Chunking for retrieval
Chunking breaks a lesson into smaller sections for retrieval. Start with headings so each chunk keeps a coherent idea. Pick a size that balances useful context with precise matching: very large chunks add noise, while very small ones can lose the explanation around a term.

## Embeddings and cosine similarity
An embedding maps text to a numeric vector. Compare a query embedding with stored chunk embeddings from the same model. Cosine similarity uses the angle between vectors to rank candidate chunks; it is not proof that a passage supports a claim.

## Citations and abstention
Keep each chunk identifier next to its source section. A citation should link to real evidence for the answer; the server can reject citation IDs that were not retrieved. If the passages do not cover the question, politely abstain rather than inventing an answer or a source.

question.prompt: Which step finds relevant lesson sections before an answer is written?
Why keep a chunk identifier next to its source section?
question.answer: To cite the exact source section.
question.rubric: Credit an answer that connects the identifier to verifiable source location or traceable citations.

question.prompt: What should the tutor do when no passage supports an answer?
options: Say the lesson does not cover it
question.answer: Say the lesson does not cover it

modules.title: LangChain workflows
modules.description: Understand how a retriever, prompt, model, and parser compose into a chain.

lessons.title: Composable chains and retrievers
lessons.content:
## Runnable composition
A runnable pipeline composes clearly defined steps. A retriever looks up evidence, a prompt template formats context, a model writes the response, and a parser checks the output. Typed inputs and outputs help you test each step independently.

## Retrievers and document metadata
A retriever accepts a search query and returns relevant documents or passages. Store document metadata such as source IDs for traceability. Filtering by lesson before ranking keeps the search inside the selected lesson.

## Testing each stage
Test a chain with fixed input and known evidence. If the final answer fails, inspect intermediate results to see whether retrieval missed the evidence or the generation step misused it. Keep interfaces stable so a model or retriever can be swapped without rewriting the chain.

question.prompt: Which component returns relevant passages for a search query?
Why keep source metadata with documents?
question.answer: To trace a passage back to its source.
question.rubric: Require reference to traceability, section IDs, or citations.

question.prompt: What helps locate a failure inside a chain?

modules.title: AI evaluation
modules.description: Measure groundedness, failures, and latency with a labelled set.

lessons.title: Evaluating grounded answers
lessons.content:
## Labelled evaluation cases
Build a labelled evaluation set with a clear expected outcome for each case. Include realistic in-scope questions and off-topic questions. Keep development examples separate from an independent test set when estimating real generalization.

## Citation correctness
Citation correctness asks whether the cited section actually supports the response. An existing citation ID is only a structural check. Human reviewers can also check claim support, which requires reading the section and the answer together.

## Latency percentiles
A median describes a typical run, while the 95th percentile highlights slow requests. Label the environment and warm-up conditions when reporting latency. Keep diagnostic outcomes and failures rather than reporting only successful runs.

question.prompt: What is stronger evidence than checking a citation ID exists?
options: Checking that the cited section supports the claim
question.answer: Checking that the cited section supports the claim

question.prompt: Why report a high latency percentile?
question.answer: To show slow-tail requests that an average can hide.
question.rubric: Credit references to slower cases or tail experience.

question.prompt: What belongs in a tutor evaluation set?

modules.title: Deployment
modules.description: Ship your learning tool with health checks, quotas, and a rollback plan.

lessons.title: Shipping an AI application
lessons.content:
## Environments and secrets
Separate local development, staging, and production environments. Store credentials in platform environment variables or a secrets manager. Values compiled into public browser bundles are not secrets. Configure each environment independently and rotate credentials when exposed.

## Health and observability
A health check reports whether the application is running; readiness can additionally test a required dependency. Log model, token usage, outcome, and latency without including sensitive prompts or identity tokens.

## Guardrails and rollback
Per-user quotas and token caps protect the budget. Publish tested changes with a version you can roll back to if errors increase. After release, watch failure rates and latency so you can catch regressions before they spread.

question.prompt: Where should private provider credentials be set?
How does readiness differ from a basic health check?
question.answer: Readiness checks whether required dependencies are available.
question.rubric: Credit references to ability to serve requests or checking required dependencies.

question.prompt: What helps limit unexpected model spend?
